h100_nvl_2026_09_05.the_reversal: The K-unroll's payoff changes between chips. On A100 it HURT the single-word lane (42.28 -> 41.94) and helped the two-pass one (38.30 -> 40.29, +5.2%); on H100 it helps both, but still asymmetrically — single-word +2.4% (63.71 -> 65.25), two-pass +7.4% (55.61 -> 59.74). The pattern is the same in both places: extra loads in flight pay only where there is arithmetic to hide behind them, and the two-pass lane is the one with arithmetic. What H100 changes is that its int8 throughput rises ~3x against ~1.7x of bandwidth, so the second dp4a stops being the thing that decides the token time.
h100_nvl_2026_09_05.scaling: llama.cpp gains 1.33x from A100 to H100 (41.79 -> 55.50). Our two-pass lane gains 1.48x (40.29 -> 59.74) and our throughput lane 1.51x (42.28 -> 63.71, or 65.25 unrolled). The newer chip suits this design better than it suits theirs.

mtp_2026_09_05.\u2605CAVEAT: 12 samples on ONE prompt, and a highly repetitive one: 'The capital of France is Paris. The capital of Germany is Berlin. The capital' is a pattern the draft head can copy. Treat 83% as an optimistic upper bound, not a general accept rate. llama.cpp reports +33-39% from MTP on ordinary text, which implies ~45-50% acceptance -- and even 50% is 1.40x, so the head is worth the verify path either way. A broader corpus measurement is owed before the number is quoted.
mtp_2026_09_05.why_this_was_measured_first: The real speedup needs a two-token VERIFY step (GEMVs batched over two positions while the GDN recurrence still advances sequentially) -- days of work whose entire payoff is (1+alpha). Measuring alpha with the draft head alone cost one pod run and no new machinery, because the golden continuation is already known.
mtp_2026_09_05.bug_found_first: An earlier run reported accept rate 0.000 with draft=0 at every step. That was a 7168-byte scratch overflow (buffers sized 2*d=10240 while the FFN hidden dff=17408 routed through them), not a property of the head. A broken draft is indistinguishable from a useless one unless the probe checks itself.

batched_h100_2026_09_05._what: Batched decode, ours vs llama.cpp, one H100 NVL, same Q8_0 checkpoint, same prompt, 128 decode steps, GPU model time only on both sides (host argmax excluded).
batched_h100_2026_09_05.correctness: OURS IS GOLDEN AT EVERY BATCH SIZE: all B sequences emit the golden 13-token stream and BATCH_AGREEMENT is perfect (32/32 at B=32). The batched kernels are bit-identical to the golden single-sequence ones (batched_equivalence_lock, 6/6).
batched_h100_2026_09_05.verdict: BATCH-1 IS OURS: 59.74 vs 56.68, and closer to the f64 oracle (1.428e-2 vs 1.499e-2), golden tokens. BATCH IS THEIRS, decisively and increasingly: llama.cpp is 1.5x ahead at B=2 and 3.76x ahead at B=32 (593.49 vs 157.70). We scale 3.9x from B=1 to B=32; they scale 10.5x.
batched_h100_2026_09_05.root_cause: Not bandwidth. At B=32 our step takes 202.9 ms to move 25.9 GB of weights = 128 GB/s, against ~3000 GB/s available -- we are COMPUTE bound. The batched GEMV keeps one warp per output row and loops BTG=8 sequences in registers, so per 512-weight block it issues ~64 dp4a and re-reads each sequence's activation slab through L2: roughly 16x more activation traffic than weight traffic. A GEMV shape running a GEMM problem.
batched_h100_2026_09_05.known_fix: int8 TENSOR-CORE GEMM. The 30B lane already has `bgk_gemm_mma` (Marlin-shaped, shared-memory staged), and batch_throughput.json records that tensor-core int8 is bit-identical (int32 exact) so the golden stream survives. The dp4a kernel was chosen deliberately to get correctness first; 157.70 is a placeholder kernel's number, not our ceiling.

tensor_core_attempt_2026_09_06.result: MEASURED LOSS. Tensor-core lowering at B=8: 43.43 tok/s aggregate (golden, 8/8 agreement) against our own GEMV lowering's 135.80 and llama.cpp's 233.41. 3x SLOWER than the kernel it was meant to replace.
tensor_core_attempt_2026_09_06.why_it_lost: Starved of parallelism at this batch. The M tile is 16, so B=8 fills half of ONE tile row: grid.y=1, and for N=16384 that is 256 blocks total against the GEMV lowering's 2048. A 132-SM H100 is not filled by 256 blocks of 256 threads.
tensor_core_attempt_2026_09_06.\u2605MY PREMISE WAS WRONG: I assumed llama.cpp switches to tensor cores at batch. It does not. ggml/src/ggml-cuda/mmq.cu:327 reads `!fp16_mma_hardware_available(cc) || ne11 < MMQ_DP4A_MAX_BATCH_SIZE` with MMQ_DP4A_MAX_BATCH_SIZE = 64 — llama.cpp uses DP4A MMQ for batch < 64 EVEN WHEN TENSOR CORES ARE AVAILABLE. At B=8/16/32, our entire measured range, they are not using tensor cores at all. Their advantage is a properly TILED dp4a kernel: shared-memory staged, 256-K steps, N tiled by 128.
tensor_core_attempt_2026_09_06.what_this_corrects: MMQ_ITER_K=256 was a real finding, but I applied it to an MMA path llama.cpp itself would not use at this batch size. The right target is our EXISTING dp4a GEMV given their staging structure — which also explains our plateau: we re-read every sequence's activation slab through L2 instead of staging it once in shared memory.
tensor_core_attempt_2026_09_06.kept_because: The MMA lowering is correct (golden at B=8) and locked equivalent to the GEMV lowering. It should win above batch 64, which is exactly where llama.cpp switches to it. It stays behind the shape rule with a raised threshold, not deleted.

staged_gemv_attempt_2026_09_09._what: Shared-memory staging of the batched GEMV activations, measured against the register-tiled kernel it was meant to replace. One H100 NVL, same checkpoint, same prompt, 128 decode steps, two-pass (golden) lane, staged and unstaged emitted from the same compiler run.
staged_gemv_attempt_2026_09_09.gpu: NVIDIA H100 NVL, 95830 MiB, sm_90, RunPod $2.59/hr
staged_gemv_attempt_2026_09_09.result: MEASURED LOSS AT EVERY BATCH SIZE, worsening with B: 66.91 vs 73.52 at B=2 (-9.0%), 103.10 vs 133.67 at B=8 (-22.9%), 85.72 vs 157.87 at B=32 (-45.7%) aggregate tok/s. Every run emitted the golden 13-token stream; BATCH_AGREEMENT 32/32 at B=32.
staged_gemv_attempt_2026_09_09.reproducibility: The unstaged B=32 lane measured 157.87 here against 157.70 recorded on a different pod on 2026-09-05 — 0.1% apart, so the harness and the chip both reproduce.
staged_gemv_attempt_2026_09_09.why_it_lost: Staging does not remove the activation reads; it converts them into a cooperative shared-memory load amortised over the block's output rows. A block is 8 warps of one row each, so the amortisation is 8x — which the L2 already provided for free: the whole activation slab is 20-320 KB against a 50 MB L2. The staged form pays two barriers per 512-element K chunk and 34 KB of shared memory per block to buy nothing, and the cost grows with B, which is why the deficit widens.
staged_gemv_attempt_2026_09_09.\u2605THE ORIGINAL DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG: batched_h100_2026_09_05.root_cause reads 're-reads each sequence's activation slab through L2: roughly 16x more activation traffic than weight traffic'. That traffic is L2-resident, not HBM, so it was never the bandwidth cost it was written up as. Two levers derived from it were built and both measured slower.

what_the_probe_showed._what: A standalone probe at the real projection shape (N=17408, K=5120) timing the one-word and two-pass GEMVs, correcting for the grid.y passes over the weights.
what_the_probe_showed.reading: At B=2 the kernel reaches 2621 GB/s of weight throughput, close to the HBM limit, so the shape is efficient where the batch is small. BTG=8 caps sequences per block, so at B=32 the weight matrix is streamed four times (grid.y=4).

btg_sweep._what: Raising BTG so one pass covers the batch removes the 4x weight re-read. Measured at the real shape, two-pass lane, milliseconds per launch.
btg_sweep.verdict: WORSE, 2.6x at B=32. The unrolled per-sequence loop holds BTG activation registers and BTG accumulators, so register pressure collapses occupancy: 40 registers at BTG=8 (full occupancy) becomes 178 at BTG=32 (~18%). No spills — it is occupancy, not spilling.

staged_gemv_attempt_2026_09_09.conclusion: BTG=8 with no staging is a genuine local optimum for the one-warp-per-row shape: both available levers measure worse, for two different and now-quantified reasons. Closing the remaining gap to llama.cpp requires its structure rather than a parameter — shared-memory tiles for BOTH operands with register blocking, which decouples tile width from per-thread register count. That is a rewrite, not a tuning change.
staged_gemv_attempt_2026_09_09.kept: Both staged kernels remain, locked bit-identical to the register-tiled originals (batched_equivalence_lock), behind LOGOS_Q38B_STAGED=1. They are correct and are the starting point for a properly tiled version; they are not the default because they are slower.

mmq_tile_2026_09_09._what: An MMQ-shaped lowering for the batched projection: both operands staged in shared memory with register blocking, replacing the one-warp-per-row register tile above a batch threshold. Measured on an isolated projection at the real shape (N=17408, K=5120) against the kernel it would replace, same data, same launch harness.
mmq_tile_2026_09_09.result: WIN ABOVE A THRESHOLD, growing with batch: 0.95x at B=16, 1.22x at B=32, 1.39x at B=64. Below the crossover a block stages a whole tile whether or not the batch fills it, so the lowering is selected by a shape rule at B>=32 rather than replacing the GEMV outright.
mmq_tile_2026_09_09.why_it_works: The register tile reuses each weight element across all B sequences but each activation element across exactly one output row — 64 activation loads per weight load at B=32. Neither escape exists inside a warp-register tile: the sequence tile must cover the batch or the weight matrix is re-streamed (4x at B=32), and rows-per-warp needs RI*BTG accumulators, measured 40 -> 63 -> 96 -> 178 registers. Shared memory decouples tile size from register count.

two_bugs_that_decided_it.thread_map: (TI/RI)*(TJ/RJ) must equal the block size or surplus threads recompute another thread's outputs — silently correct, 4x the work. Now a static_assert.
two_bugs_that_decided_it.bank_conflicts: Unpadded shared rows are KC bytes apart and shared memory repeats every 128 B, so every thread of a warp hit one bank: a 32-way conflict on every read of the inner loop. One int of padding took the kernel from 0.704 to 0.450 ms on the development card — the difference between losing and winning.

mmq_tile_2026_09_09.negative_result_cp_async: Double-buffering the tile with cp.async gave NO benefit: 1.20x against the plain tile's 1.22x at B=32. The +1-int padding that removes the bank conflicts also breaks the 16-byte alignment a wide cp.async needs, so the copies fall back to 4 bytes, and the second buffer costs 51 KB per block which halves occupancy. Not pursued.
mmq_tile_2026_09_09.parameters_confirmed_against_llama_cpp: A sweep of the staged K chunk over 128/256/512 independently selected 256, which is llama.cpp's MMQ_ITER_K; 8 warps per block is what the thread budget wants. Accumulation in double is free on this part (fp64 half-rate; 1.22x with double against 1.25x with float) and 10x more accurate, but would be wrong on a consumer card where fp64 is 1/32 rate — so it is a knob.
mmq_tile_2026_09_09.status: LANDED AND VERIFIED. The emitter's shape rule selects the tile at batch >= 32 and emits byte-identically the kernel that was measured. tensor_core_tile_2026_09_09._what: The batched projection lowered onto the TENSOR CORES: mma.sync.m16n8k32.s8 in place of __dp4a, on the same shared-memory staged tile. The instruction consumes exactly 32 K-elements, which is exactly one Q8_0 block, so the quantisation scale still lands on an instruction boundary and nothing about the numerics has to move.
tensor_core_tile_2026_09_09.why_dp4a_could_not_get_there: Ablation against the MMQ-tile step put the GEMM at 79.1 ms of a 93.4 ms step (84.7%). The work is 1.557e12 int8 MACs (two passes over 24.33 GB of weights at batch 32); against 132 SMs x 256 dp4a MAC/clk that is 26.3 ms at 100% efficiency, and the step budget that beats llama.cpp is 39.7 ms of GEMM. Measured efficiency was 39%, and no dp4a shape recovers the rest: raising operand reuse from 1.33 to 4.00 (RI=8, RJ=4) measured 0.96x, because the taller tile starves the machine of blocks faster than it saves shared-memory loads. The tensor cores run the same MACs at 1024/SM/clk.

levers_measured_separately.mma_vs_dp4a: 1.5x-1.9x per shape at the same tile
levers_measured_separately.KC_128_vs_256: uniform win, +12% to +21%: a shallower staged chunk keeps more blocks resident
levers_measured_separately.split_K: the decisive one on narrow shapes -- N=5120 is 128 of the 257 launches and gives 40 blocks of the 128-row tile, leaving 70% of the SMs idle; splitting K is worth 2.5x there
levers_measured_separately.weight_prefetch: 1.27x on the deep-K shape (K=17408); overlaps HBM latency with the mma
levers_measured_separately.int32_scale_combine: REJECTED -- predicted to halve the quarter-rate cvt.rn.f32.s32 count, measured 1-2% SLOWER at every shape and less faithful to the shipped arithmetic, so the two-cvt grouping was kept

tensor_core_tile_2026_09_09.split_rule: split = clamp(ceil(1024 / (N/TI)), 1, 16) capped at half the staged chunks. Within 1% of a per-shape hand-tuned table (33.6 ms vs 33.2 ms of GEMM per step), so the rule is the artifact rather than the table.

small_batch_campaign_2026_09_09.how_llama_cpp_wins_at_small_batch: Read from ggml/src/ggml-cuda/mmvq.cu rather than inferred. Their edge is not the instruction, it is REDUCTION WIDTH: calc_nwarps gives 4 warps at ncols_dst<=4 and 2 at <=8, with calc_rows_per_block = 2. With time split roughly half and half, neither half alone suffices (~1.3x each): TMA on the data side AND ldmatrix plus register reuse on the compute side -- the tile currently loads every mma fragment with FOUR scalar shared loads.

compute_half_priced._what: All six shared fragment loads per mma replaced with constants (timing only).
compute_half_priced.reading: ldmatrix is worth LESS than 5% -- it reduces these loads, it does not remove them.

root_cause.finding: The ~53% mma phase on Hopper is the Q8_0 PER-BLOCK RESCALE, not the loads or the mma issues. Per thread per 128-K chunk: 16 mma.sync issues against 64 int32->float convert+scale+accumulate -- a 4:1 ratio, because Q8_0 carries a scale every 32 elements.
root_cause.why_vllm_has_no_equivalent: Hopper fp8 tensor cores accumulate in fp32 natively and apply one scale at the end.
root_cause.route: fp8 weights on Hopper. chip.rs has listed Precision::Fp8 for Hopper/Blackwell since the start and the emitter has never used it. Must be priced against the f64 oracle before shipping: fp8 e4m3 carries ~4 mantissa bits where our int8 carries 8.

fp8_hypothesis_priced_and_rejected._what: Per-32-block rescale replaced by one end-of-K accumulate (timing only) -- what fp8 buys.
fp8_hypothesis_priced_and_rejected.reading: +4%, not the 1.8x the op-count model predicted. The ~53% 'mma' phase is neither the shared loads nor the rescale: clock64 measures WALL time, so it is dominated by implicit memory stalls during compute. The tile is memory-system-bound end to end.

verdict.conclusion: This tile cannot reach B=32 parity, measured rather than asserted. The three levers with any headroom are CEILINGS obtained by deleting the work, not by optimising it. Winning B=32 needs TMA + wgmma + an async epilogue as ONE dataflow -- a CUTLASS-class kernel -- which the wgmma experiment already showed cannot be reached piecewise.

gate.name: where_q4_is_lossless_it_equals_the_int8_tile_exactly
gate.idea: the requantiser scales each block by its own max, so at max==7 the nibble IS the int8 value and the scales match -- the lanes must then agree BIT FOR BIT. Turns a lossy format into an exactly-checkable one; a tolerance would have passed the fp8 tile that measured rel_L2 1.001.

bugs_caught: the two-mask nibble expansion (lo|hi<<8) collides: K2 and K1 land in the same byte

v - 0x08080808 is a 32-BIT subtract and BORROWS ACROSS BYTES -- every nibble below 8 decremented the next K-element, off-by-one on 37% of values, indistinguishable from quantisation noise in an accuracy number. Fixed with __vsub4.
q4_lane_2026_09_21.verdict: SLOWER as staged despite moving 47% less. Expanding nibbles needs COMPUTE between the global read and the shared store, which cp.async cannot do, so the lane gives up the async pipeline and that costs more than the traffic saves.
q4_lane_2026_09_21.what_would_make_it_pay: cp.async the PACKED nibbles into a half-size shared tile and expand at the FRAGMENT LOAD. Keeps the async pipeline, halves shared memory too, moves ~4 ALU into the mma loop -- and rewrites the fragment-load indexing, which is exactly where re-derivation produced a wrong kernel twice today, so it belongs behind the exact gate that now exists.

second_arrangement._what: packed staged through cp.async, expanded at the fragment load; passed the exact gate first try
second_arrangement.why_worse: the tile's 8 warps are 2 row-groups x 4 column-groups and all four column-warps read the SAME A rows, so expanding at the fragment load repeats the work 4x -- 64 expansions per thread per chunk against 16 at staging, ~44 ALU ops per mma issue.
second_arrangement.verdict: Q4 loses in BOTH arrangements: pay the unpack once and lose the async pipeline, or keep the pipeline and pay it four times. A third (cp.async packed, expand shared->shared) costs 1.5x shared memory, and occupancy is the lever that has mattered most.

third_arrangement._what: cp.async packed + ONE cooperative shared->shared expansion; mma loop untouched; gate passed first try
third_arrangement.cost: 1.5x shared memory (sP beside sW); at KC=128 it overruns the static budget outright
third_arrangement.verdict: ALL THREE arrangements lose. Pay the unpack once and lose the pipeline (+27%), four times and keep it (+78%), or once and keep it at the cost of the shared memory that buys occupancy (+33%). There is no fourth place to put the work -- Q4 is closed.
